title: Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee, 3–5 August 2026
summary:
The MPC unanimously kept the repo rate at 5.25% and retained a neutral stance. The standing deposit facility stayed at 5.00% and the marginal standing facility and Bank Rate at 5.50%. June headline CPI had risen to 4.4%, primarily from food and fuel, while core inflation was steady at 3.9% over May and June. Excluding precious metals, the resolution puts core inflation in a 2.3–2.5% range over those months. The committee saw limited spread of price pressures so far and was watching whether higher input costs would move into other prices.

The MPC projected 6.7% real GDP growth and 5.0% CPI inflation in fiscal 2026–27, with inflation reaching 5.9% in Q3. The decision weighs domestic consumption, infrastructure and credit growth against weather risks and uncertainty about oil and trade. A weaker monsoon could raise food prices while hurting rural demand. The committee held while seeking evidence on the makeup and persistence of inflation.

questions.question: Is the evidence of limited cost pass-through consistent across sectors?
questions.evidence: Compare CPI diffusion, firm selling-price surveys and wage measures with input costs.

questions.question: What happens to consumption if the weaker monsoon reduces rural income?
questions.evidence: Compare rainfall, agricultural production and rural spending using consistent regional coverage.

questions.question: Which upcoming data can change the expected repo path?
questions.evidence: Compare policy-sensitive OIS across dated releases and identify shocks from contemporaneous survey expectations.

locator: Resolution paragraphs 2 and 4–17; charts 1 and 2 correspond to the growth and inflation projections stated in the text.

title: Indonesia’s Economy Grows 5.29% in Second Quarter of 2026
summary:
Bank Indonesia reported 5.29% year-on-year real GDP growth in the second quarter, following 5.61% in the previous quarter, and kept its full-year forecast range at 4.9–5.7%. It attributes Q2 growth primarily to domestic spending. Household consumption grew 5.06%, reflecting in part school holidays and religious holidays. Government consumption grew 15.97%, with salary timing and programme procurement contributing. Investment and exports grew, supported by vehicle investment, public and private projects and trade partner demand.

On the production side, Bank Indonesia cited strength in manufacturing, trade, construction, information and communication, and accommodation and food services. The release separates activity realised in Q2 from its forecast of ongoing domestic demand support. The timing of salaries, school holidays and government purchases matters when using a single quarter to judge underlying demand.

questions.question: How much consumer growth survives adjustments for calendar and fiscal effects?
questions.evidence: Compare seasonally adjusted consumption, retail activity and government payments with the same quarter’s raw levels.

questions.question: Is investment demand broadening outside vehicle purchases?
questions.evidence: Review gross fixed capital formation by asset type and separate projects financed by the public sector.

questions.question: Which export industries contributed to real output and local demand?
questions.evidence: Compare trade weights and production volumes with import intensity and domestic value added.

locator: Release paragraphs on GDP, expenditure components, production sectors and annual outlook.

title: Economic and Financial Developments in Malaysia in the Second Quarter of 2026
summary:
Bank Negara Malaysia reported that GDP growth strengthened to 6.0% year on year, from 5.4% in the first quarter. Seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter growth was 2.5%. BNM links the expansion to steady income and policy support for households, investment activity and exports. It identifies technology-related electrical and electronics exports and services as areas of sustained strength, with a rebound in LNG and other manufactured shipments adding support.

Headline inflation climbed to 1.9% as fuel costs increased. Core inflation eased to 1.9% from 2.1%, with BNM pointing to jewellery, watches and rent among the drivers. BNM observed that higher producer costs were mostly upstream and reported limited pass-through across broader consumer prices. The share of items with monthly price increases rose to 45.5%, near the stated historical average, with an April rise followed by moderation. The growth, inflation level and diffusion figures are separate measures.

questions.question: How much of the stronger GDP reading reflects a sustained trend in domestic demand?
questions.evidence: Compare seasonally adjusted consumption and investment by component with export and import volumes.

questions.question: Are upstream costs starting to reach consumer categories beyond fuel?
questions.evidence: Compare producer and retail price series and update the monthly CPI diffusion measure.

questions.question: Does stronger technology demand create durable income growth locally?
questions.evidence: Examine employment, value-added shares and net exports in the segments seeing the strongest capital spending.

locator: Release sections on quarterly activity, inflation and currency conditions; embargo dated 14 August 2026.

title: Overseas Filipino Remittances: June 2026 release table
summary:
The BSP release table records June personal remittances at US$3.388 billion, up 1.8% from June a year earlier, and cash remittances through banks at US$3.039 billion, up 1.7%. January–June cash remittances reached US$17.149 billion, 2.4% above the corresponding prior-year period. The seasonally adjusted personal remittance series rose 0.4% month on month in June.

Personal and cash remittances cover different flows. The source defines personal remittances more broadly, including certain non-cash transfers and net compensation. The peso value reaching households can move differently from these dollar totals, so household purchasing power depends on conversion rates and prices. The 2026 table rows are labelled preliminary.

questions.question: Do the monthly data signal sustained acceleration or a calendar effect?
questions.evidence: Compare longer runs of the seasonally adjusted personal series across vintages.

questions.question: How much purchasing power did these inflows represent for households?
questions.evidence: Convert by period exchange rates and deflate using an appropriate consumer price series.

questions.question: How concentrated is remittance growth across sources?
questions.evidence: Compare origin countries, channels and overseas employment data to identify common vulnerabilities.

locator: BSP release annex dated 17 August in the archive filename. 2026 June monthly/cumulative rows and the personal, cash and seasonal adjustment definition notes.

title: End-July 2026 GIR settle at US$103.3B; BOP posts US$1.5-B deficit in July 2026
summary:
The BSP reported a July balance-of-payments deficit of US$1.5 billion and a cumulative January–July deficit of US$5.3 billion. It attributes the cumulative deficit to merchandise trade and foreign portfolio outflows, partly cushioned by remittances, government borrowing, services trade and inward direct investment.

End-July gross international reserves were revised to US$103.3 billion from US$104.7 billion at end-June. The BSP attributes the decrease to factors including its net FX operations, the government’s reserve-related flows and valuation effects, partially offset by foreign investment income and higher gold valuations. Its reserve-coverage measures were 6.7 months of relevant imports and payments and about 3.7 times short-term external debt on a residual-maturity basis. The two ratios use different denominators. The release separates movements in the reserve stock from the overall balance-of-payments flow.

questions.question: How much of the monthly reserve loss can be traced to FX transactions?
questions.evidence: Reconcile net reserve transactions, market valuation, investment income and government account movements.

questions.question: Is the year-to-date external deficit narrowing because of durable improvement?
questions.evidence: Compare trade volumes, prices, financing and remittances over the same seasonal windows.

questions.question: What if short-term external repayments rose?
questions.evidence: Use a residual-maturity schedule to test changes in the reserves-to-debt ratio under alternative flows.

locator: Dated release text and notes 1–2. The BSP page is rendered dynamically; the publisher’s dated indexed version supplies the release text.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting, 3–5 August 2026
summary:
The August minutes show that all six members favoured retaining the repo rate at 5.25%. Their reasons illuminate the conditions behind the neutral stance. Nagesh Kumar cites stronger capacity utilisation and investment despite risks from weather, trade and energy. Poonam Gupta points to an improved oil assumption and a marginally lower inflation forecast, while judging that a case for a hike could emerge if inflation proved persistent. Sanjay Malhotra sees little evidence of widespread inflation so far and would wait for better evidence on where inflation is settling.

The minutes explain the timing problem. A hold kept room to respond to adverse supply shocks while evidence on second-round effects developed. Indranil Bhattacharyya’s statement describes the value of communicating the conditions for future moves in an uncertain environment. Gupta cites about US$90 per barrel as a reasonable assumption for the fiscal year using oil futures available then. This is a forecasting assumption, and the minutes themselves are a later release about an earlier decision.

questions.question: Which inflation components would cause members to converge on a hike?
questions.evidence: Compare individual reaction conditions with forward revisions, diffusion and survey expectations.

questions.question: How sensitive is the difference between the June and August forecasts to the oil assumption?
questions.evidence: Use the published model assumptions to compare effects from oil, weather and other forecast changes.

questions.question: Did publication of individual views change market pricing beyond the meeting-day decision?
questions.evidence: Compare OIS quotes around the minutes release, isolating other scheduled announcements.

locator: Member vote and individual statements, including Gupta paragraphs 47–52, Malhotra paragraphs 53–57 and the discussion of framework guidance.

title: BI-Rate Held at 5.75%: Strengthening Stability, Supporting Economic Growth
summary:
Bank Indonesia held the BI-Rate at 5.75%, with the Deposit Facility at 4.75% and Lending Facility at 6.50%. The bank described rupiah stability and keeping inflation inside its 2.5% ± 1 percentage point corridor as objectives. The release anticipated above-10% primary money growth as part of maintaining adequate liquidity while other tools addressed volatility from abroad.

The bank expanded eligibility for a 12.5% hedging-swap premium reduction. In addition to qualifying portfolio inflows, the measure opened eligibility to qualifying foreign loans by banks and foreign direct investment, with the new transactions due to take effect in the second week of September. It also anticipated macroprudential liquidity incentives to redistribute liquidity and support lending. The release ties the FX intervention and hedging measures to stabilisation, while reserve and credit measures aim to preserve domestic funding.

questions.question: Did broader eligibility lower all-in funding costs for eligible borrowers?
questions.evidence: Compare swap pricing including the premium incentive with alternatives at matched tenor.

questions.question: Did the change alter the composition of foreign flows?
questions.evidence: Distinguish portfolio flows, foreign borrowing and FDI alongside new eligible hedging transactions.

questions.question: Did money-market liquidity reach smaller lenders?
questions.evidence: Compare transaction depth, INDONIA and facility usage by participant type after implementation.

locator: Release 28/162/DKom, decision and policy-mix measures 1–3.

title: Monetary Policy Committee’s Decision 4/2026
summary:
The MPC voted unanimously to keep the policy rate at 1.00%. It judged the accommodative stance and targeted financial measures helpful for a recovery that was still uneven. Technology and AI supported exports and investment. The committee cautioned that imported inputs limited the domestic benefit and that consumption had been weaker than anticipated amid high living costs.

The MPC revised its headline inflation assessment down for 2026 and 2027, mainly reflecting global energy prices. It expected price pressures to rise temporarily through the first quarter of 2027 as El Niño and cost pass-through took effect. It described medium-term inflation expectations as anchored and noted that larger firms led credit growth while SME loans continued to contract. Much of the larger-firm credit demand concerned working capital. The committee encouraged targeted measures for vulnerable borrowers.

questions.question: How much export and investment growth becomes domestic value added?
questions.evidence: Compare electronics orders and capital goods imports with value added and employment.

questions.question: Would higher energy or food costs lift underlying inflation expectations?
questions.evidence: Track CPI diffusion, subsidy adjustments and medium-term expectations against the projected peak.

questions.question: Is the working capital pickup a sign of demand or rising input costs?
questions.evidence: Compare new loan applications and uses with inventories, margins and borrower sizes.

locator: Press Release 31/2026, decision, outlook, inflation and financial conditions paragraphs.

title: Monetary and Financial Developments in July 2026
summary:
Bank Negara Malaysia reported that headline and core inflation both fell to 1.8% from 1.9% in June. The bank attributes the headline moderation partly to slower retail fuel inflation, with subsidised diesel and lower RON97 prices relevant to the comparison. It identifies softer health insurance and jewellery and watches inflation as contributors to the core reading.

The trade surplus widened to RM22.5 billion while export and import growth both slowed from high June readings. Technology demand continued to support electronics shipments. Business lending growth picked up, mainly in working capital, while household loan growth held at 5.3%. BNM also reported an aggregate liquidity coverage ratio of 148.7%, distinct from loan performance or conditions at individual institutions. Its account of the July market describes a rise in Malaysian equities amid non-resident inflows and positive domestic growth expectations. That observation is for July, before the release.

questions.question: How much of disinflation depends on fuel subsidies or one-off core categories?
questions.evidence: Rebuild CPI contributions under prevailing and alternative administered-price assumptions.

questions.question: Does slower import growth foreshadow investment moderation?
questions.evidence: Compare capital import volumes with domestic investment data and machinery order timing.

questions.question: Does working-capital growth reflect stress or expansion?
questions.evidence: Compare inventory needs, borrower sales and arrears with new credit by sector.

locator: Inflation, trade, private credit, bank liquidity and domestic markets sections; notes 1–2 define core inflation and fuel subsidy context.

title: Economic and Monetary Conditions for July 2026
summary:
The Bank of Thailand assessed that economic activity improved in July from June. Electronics exports and manufacturing benefited from global demand linked to the technology cycle, with exports relying heavily on imported inputs. Private investment softened after earlier strength. The bank attributes improved tourism and services activity to higher arrivals and flight capacity, while government measures and the extended holiday supported some domestic services spending.

Headline inflation fell as domestic fuel prices declined and contributions to the Oil Fuel Fund fell. Core inflation rose slightly, with prepared food and cooking inputs contributing to cost pass-through. The current-account deficit narrowed, in part because gold and fuel imports fell. These observations give different signals about external demand, domestic spending and underlying price pressure. The monthly release flags the durability of the technology cycle, tourism and weather among the uncertainties.

questions.question: Are the technology exports adding domestic income in proportion to their growth?
questions.evidence: Compare gross exports with imported input shares, jobs and domestic value added.

questions.question: Will the tourism pickup continue when holiday and flight-capacity effects fade?
questions.evidence: Track arrival composition, booked seats, length of stay and visitor spending.

questions.question: Does the headline/core divergence reflect sustained pass-through?
questions.evidence: Compare fresh food, fuel and prepared-food movements with producer costs and subsidy conditions.

locator: Release 34/2026, July summary and detail. Note focuses on the release text and omits the separate statistical tables.

title: CPI in August 2026 Remains Under Control
summary:
August CPI inflation rose 0.21% month on month and 3.19% year on year, within Bank Indonesia’s target corridor. Annual core inflation rose from 2.76% to 2.92%. The bank highlights gold jewellery as an important contributor to monthly core inflation. Volatile food inflation accelerated, led in part by chicken, chillies and rice. The bank observed a fall in administered prices over the month, principally in selected airfares and fuels.

The release attributes inflation remaining within target partly to coordination with regional and central government inflation teams. It expects inflation to stay inside the corridor in 2026 and 2027. The mix of food, selected regulated prices and jewellery matters because their contribution says less about broad demand-driven inflation than a similarly sized movement spread across the basket.

questions.question: How broad was the August core pickup after stripping out gold jewellery?
questions.evidence: Check item weights, component contributions and median price inflation.

questions.question: Which food price increases are seasonal or tied to supply?
questions.evidence: Compare crop output, local distribution and wholesale data with seasonal price profiles.

questions.question: How exposed is the outlook to future fare and fuel resets?
questions.evidence: Track administered price schedules and energy costs, then compare their likely pass-through to services.

locator: Release 28/176/DKom, headline CPI, core, volatile food and administered prices paragraphs.

title: Monetary Policy Statement
summary:
The MPC held its Overnight Policy Rate at 2.75%. The statement reports first-half growth of 5.7%, supported by stronger-than-expected exports and sustained domestic demand, and expects full-year growth of around 5%. It attributes resilience to technology-linked exports, tourism and continued investment. A prolonged Middle East conflict or lower commodity production would weigh on the outlook, while firmer technology demand or tourism could support it.

Headline and core inflation averaged 1.8% and 2.0% in the first seven months, respectively. The committee saw only limited pass-through to consumer prices despite higher costs and strong growth, partly because export strength had spilled only modestly into wages. It kept the rate at a level it judged consistent with price stability and growth, and continued monitoring the balance between cost pressures and domestic demand.

questions.question: Would stronger export orders lift wages enough to change inflation pressure?
questions.evidence: Use sectoral wage and employment data against export production, controlling for the difference between output and local value added.

questions.question: How much downside growth risk comes from lower commodity volumes?
questions.evidence: Distinguish production outages from price changes and track trade and investment spillovers.

questions.question: How much of the decision and forecast tone was already in prices?
questions.evidence: Use timestamped MYR quotes or policy-sensitive rates around the published embargo with meeting expectations recorded beforehand.

locator: Opening decision and domestic growth and inflation paragraphs; 3 September embargo.

title: Taming the Impact of Supply Shocks: The Philippine Economic Outlook
summary:
Deputy Governor Zeno Ronald R. Abenoja’s Hong Kong briefing presented cooling August inflation alongside a projected rise later in the year. The contribution chart ties the moderation to food, while the forecast chart shows a later peak under the baseline. The survey slide draws on 21 analysts surveyed by 20 August and distinguishes one- and three-year-ahead expectations. These observations describe the briefing’s data and survey vintages.

The policy-rate chart shows a rise to 5.0% by the August meeting. The BSP’s accompanying slide describes the August increase as a way to anchor expectations and contain second-round effects. The combination of easing near-term inflation and a higher policy rate reflects concern about the forecast path and the transmission of supply shocks. This note uses the opening-remarks slides as published, which can be reviewed alongside the corresponding speech recording if available.

questions.question: What separates the later inflation peak from the contemporaneous easing in food prices?
questions.evidence: Recreate the contributions and base effects assumed in the forecast, including alternate food and energy paths.

questions.question: How robust is the change in private economists’ expectations?
questions.evidence: Check respondent coverage and the dispersion behind the survey averages.

questions.question: Did local funding rates move with the policy rate after the August decision?
questions.evidence: Compare matched-tenor market rates and lending indicators using their time and frequency metadata.

locator: Briefing slides headed “Inflation eased further in August”, the quarterly inflation forecast, analyst expectations and “Measured policy rate increase”.

title: Governor’s Welcoming Address at the Dinner Commemorating 30th Anniversary of FAST
summary:
The address, delivered by Deputy Governor Marzunisham Omar for Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour, sets out Bank Negara Malaysia’s plans to update debt-market infrastructure. FAST moved issuance and tendering electronically. The address reports that the domestic bond and sukuk market was about RM2.35 trillion at end-June 2026 and that more than RM377 billion was raised in the corporate bond market from January 2025 to June 2026. These figures describe a market stock and cumulative fundraising, respectively.

BNM expects FAST+ and the next-generation scripless depository to support issuing, settling and holding tokenised debt. It announced a planned soft launch for SSDS+ on 25 September. This is a prospective market infrastructure change with possible implications for issuance and operations. The speech offers no measured effect on liquidity or issuance costs at the time of delivery.

questions.question: Does the platform change lead times or issuance costs for corporate debt?
questions.evidence: Compare matched issues before and after adoption, controlling for borrower and market conditions.

questions.question: How do tokenised instruments settle and remain interoperable with existing securities?
questions.evidence: Review published settlement rules, cash-leg mechanics and participant eligibility.

questions.question: Does new issuance broaden or concentrate market access?
questions.evidence: Track issuers, issue sizes, syndicates and secondary turnover by instrument type.

locator: FAST history, debt market figures and FAST+/SSDS+ launch paragraphs.

title: Edited Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting No. 4/2026
summary:
The September publication reviews the August meeting and its decision to retain accommodation. The committee discussed the limited spillover from technology exports, weaker household purchasing power and vulnerable balance sheets. Growth in some areas coexisted with weak aggregate momentum. The members considered the ability of credit policy and targeted support to reach specific borrowers as distinct from aggregate monetary stimulus.

The minutes detail the temporary inflation impulse expected from supply costs despite a lower forecast than previously assessed. The Secretariat noted that the Oil Fuel Fund might cushion sharp oil-price increases for one to three months, while the committee emphasised uncertainty about the broader price and supply-chain response. The baht moved with external policy expectations and geopolitical news, while the committee saw credit weakness concentrated in SMEs. The discussion provides the conditions behind the unchanged setting without attaching a timetable for future rate changes.

questions.question: How would lower oil-subsidy capacity change the inflation path?
questions.evidence: Reconcile retail price rules, Oil Fuel Fund capacity and oil price scenarios.

questions.question: When do technological exports spill into labour income and consumption?
questions.evidence: Compare employer-sector wages and household spending with export and capital-goods data.

questions.question: Can targeted financing restore healthy credit to SMEs?
questions.evidence: Measure approval, credit costs and loan performance for eligible and otherwise similar firms.

locator: Edited minutes pp. 1–4, economic and inflation assessment, financial conditions and monetary policy considerations.

title: Monetary Policy Report – August 2026
summary:
The BSP’s August-edition report records a 25 basis point increase in the target reverse repurchase rate to 5.0% on 27 August. The Monetary Board saw a case for a measured tightening to protect expectations despite weak recent activity. Current and projected inflation told different stories. July inflation eased from 6.4% to 6.2% owing to fuel and some services, and lower-than-expected midyear readings helped bring the 2026 forecast down to 6.1%. In contrast, the 2027 and 2028 forecasts were revised higher because of the potential agricultural effects of El Niño and higher minimum wage assumptions. Near-term output weakness reflected a smaller-than-expected Q2 GDP reading, with recovery projected for 2027.

The report’s scenarios show how forecasts can change with the persistence of supply shocks, the scope of wage adjustments and domestic demand. Its higher inflation scenario examines oil stress and rice supply, while the lower inflation case includes more localised wage changes and softer spending. Professional forecasters reported lower inflation expectations in August, though the 12-month measure stayed above the upper bound of the target range. The report presents that survey evidence separately from the BSP forecast. The policy decision addresses prospective inflation and expectations, while the report gives conditional paths for growth and prices.

questions.question: How much of the medium-term upward revision comes from the wage assumption?
questions.evidence: Reconcile forecast changes by oil, food and wage assumptions and compare registered wage changes and pass-through.

questions.question: What would make below-target growth the binding policy consideration?
questions.evidence: Compare alternative outputs under different real income, investment and rate paths using the forecast assumptions.

questions.question: Could the survey average mask disagreement on the inflation horizon?
questions.evidence: Examine respondent dispersion, response timing and conditions for the return to target.

locator: Monetary policy summary, Economic Outlook tables and scenarios, and July inflation and forecast survey sections. August edition published 11 September per the BSP release calendar; selected sections and exhibits reviewed.

title: The Indian Economy in an Ever More Volatile and Complex World
summary:
Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta argues that India has absorbed several external shocks at once, including energy disruption, trade uncertainty and El Niño risk. She describes policy as initially aimed at securing essential supplies, then allowing some energy costs to reach consumers as the shock persisted. She links resilience to domestic consumption and investment, export diversification and fiscal discipline. The IMF public-debt projection she cites is an external forecast.

Gupta sees a divergence across markets. In her assessment, government bonds benefited from fiscal credibility and sustained growth prospects, while equities had a weaker relative run following earlier gains. She distinguishes the current account’s structural services and remittance support from commodity-import costs and shifts in capital flows. She cites a 13.0% point-to-point rupee depreciation from 31 March 2025 to 17 September 2026. Her prospective adjustment in the balance of payments depends on expectations about future trade and asset flows. The historical currency move predates the speech.

questions.question: How much of the external gap reflects oil and gold prices versus underlying volumes?
questions.evidence: Separate import valuation and real volumes, with services receipts and remittances on the same basis.

questions.question: What would induce a durable recovery in foreign portfolio flows?
questions.evidence: Compare valuation and earnings revisions with FX-hedged returns and allocation flows across peers.

questions.question: How sensitive is fiscal room to higher borrowing costs?
questions.evidence: Test debt dynamics under alternative effective interest costs and nominal-growth paths, distinguishing those scenarios from the quoted IMF projection.

locator: Section II and the discussion of bond, equity and foreign-exchange markets, including footnotes 2–5.

title: BI-Rate Held at 5.75%: Strengthening Stability, Supporting Economic Growth
summary:
Bank Indonesia held its policy rate and standing facilities at 5.75%, 4.75% and 6.50%. The bank maintained its emphasis on rupiah stabilisation with external headwinds and a 2.5% ± 1 percentage point inflation target. It described using offshore non-deliverable forwards, domestic forwards and spot transactions, and expanded reductions to premiums on eligible hedging swaps. The revised discounts were 15%, 20% and 25% on three-, six- and twelve-month tenors, respectively. The tenor schedule changes the relative incentive to hedge longer funding exposures.

The bank reported the rupiah at IDR 17,855 per US dollar on 22 September, 0.78% weaker than at end-August, and noted that end-August reserves covered 5.4 months of imports by its measure. These are pre-decision observations. The maintained policy rate coexisted with changes to implementation and continued macroprudential credit support.

questions.question: How did take-up vary by tenor after the premium schedule changed?
questions.evidence: Compare eligible hedge volumes, maturities and all-in costs with the pre-change schedule.

questions.question: Which USD/IDR exposures were driving the need for stabilisation?
questions.evidence: Compare trade and portfolio flows alongside information on market liquidity and forward curves.

questions.question: How much policymaking space does reserve adequacy provide under stress?
questions.evidence: Compare short-term external obligations, potential capital outflows and alternative import-cover paths.

locator: Press release 28/193/DKom, opening policy decision, policy measures 1–3 and balance of payments and FX assessment. The signed English dateline and Indonesian publication both show 23 September.

title: State of the Economy, September 2026
summary:
The Bulletin authors describe resilient Indian demand alongside a more challenging external environment. They cite 7.8% year-on-year GDP growth in Q1 of fiscal 2026–27, driven by consumption and investment, and strengthening food, fuel and core price pressures in August. August headline CPI reached 4.8% in their account. Near-term demand indicators and the monthly inflation readings capture different aspects of the cycle. Net services income and remittances helped contain the first-quarter current-account deficit, while foreign portfolio flows shifted from inflows in August to outflows in September to the authors’ cutoff.

The financial-conditions section shows why short-term funding and sovereign yields can diverge. System liquidity rose after use of the RBI’s swap facility linked to foreign currency non-resident bank deposits, then moderated with tax-related outflows. Commercial paper and certificate-of-deposit yields softened during the liquidity surge before firming. Government yields had already moved higher amid rising US yields, oil volatility and geopolitical risk. The authors’ discussion links those developments with funding conditions, and the charts present market levels with dates and tenors rather than identifying event reactions.

questions.question: How persistent is the liquidity created by the deposit swap facility?
questions.evidence: Reconcile swap tenors, tax outflows, government balances and durable liquidity over subsequent maintenance periods.

questions.question: Why did government yields rise when private money-market yields initially softened?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity-matched price changes and the effects of liquidity, duration supply and global yields.

questions.question: Which inflation pressures are domestic demand effects?
questions.evidence: Decompose food, fuel and core changes and check against measures of selling prices and demand.

locator: Introduction and Sections III–IV, including chart references IV.1–IV.3 and footnotes on liquidity and market observations. Focused read of the domestic and financial-conditions sections.

title: Economic and Monetary Conditions for August 2026
summary:
The Bank of Thailand saw August activity as broadly stable from July. Technology demand kept merchandise exports excluding gold at a high level, although technology shipments moderated from their earlier pace. Machinery and equipment investment strengthened, while production and service activity softened. Foreign tourist numbers rose, supported by Chinese arrivals in the bank’s account, but shorter stays held tourism receipts broadly steady.

The bank attributes higher headline inflation to fresh food affected by weather and input costs and more expensive retail fuel. It also reports a rise in core inflation, particularly as prepared-food prices reflected cost pass-through. A trade surplus supported the current-account surplus. The bank saw a broadly stable labour market and flagged the increase in unemployment-benefit claimants. A monthly trade and investment improvement can coexist with weak labour indicators or uneven production.

questions.question: How much do data-centre imports explain the difference between spending and domestic production?
questions.evidence: Trace capital equipment volumes, inventories and local construction activity to the corresponding investment measures.

questions.question: Which firms are raising prepared-food prices and which absorb higher input costs?
questions.evidence: Compare producer inputs, restaurant price surveys and household inflation by category.

questions.question: Is the rise in unemployment claims specific to certain sectors?
questions.evidence: Look at claims, employment and wage changes by sector, firm size and region.

locator: Release 37/2026, summary and August detail. Note focuses on the release text and omits the separate statistical tables.
